headline: The growth hormone research
body: And almost everyone quoting it only shows you one half.
punch: Both halves are real studies. That's what makes this interesting.

headline: Two camps
body: One says GH reliably adds height in short kids. The other says it does nothing, or makes things worse. Neither side is making its evidence up.
punch: The disagreement is inside the literature, not between honest and dishonest people.

headline: Side one
body: Meta-analyses of kids with idiopathic short stature: treated groups ended up 0.84 standard deviations taller than controls. Roughly four to six centimetres of adult height.
punch: That's the number the field usually quotes.

headline: Side two
body: A 1997 study of boys who were short but not GH deficient: untreated reached 162.0 cm on average. GH treated reached 154.2 cm. The treated boys ended up shorter.
punch: Nearly eight centimetres, in the wrong direction.

headline: So how are both true
body: Different populations and different designs. Pooled analyses lean on idiopathic short stature groups, many uncontrolled. The bad results come from controlled comparisons in non deficient boys through puberty.
punch: Who got studied changes the answer completely.

headline: Which is the actual lesson
body: Not that GH works. Not that it doesn't. That the effect depends on who you are, and nobody quoting you a single number has told you which group it came from.
punch: Ask which cohort the number came from. Every time.

headline: And the cost
body: Where gains do happen they run to roughly thirty five thousand dollars per inch of adult height.
punch: Years of daily injections for less than one shoe size.

headline: For people of normal height
subhead: THERE IS NO DATA AT ALL
body: No trial has tested GH for height in normal statured people because nobody would run it. Both camps above studied short children.
punch: If a number exists for that group, somebody made it up.

headline: What I got wrong
body: First I said GH can't work if you're not deficient. Then I overcorrected and said the meta-analyses settled it. Both were too clean. The literature is genuinely split.
punch: Getting it right matters more than sounding certain.
